summary: Explains why choosing random values that resist a determined adversary is hard, points out pitfalls of ordinary pseudo-random generators, and recommends truly random hardware sources. It has been replaced by RFC 4086.

eli5.summary: If you pick a secret number in a predictable way, a sneaky person can guess it. This note explains how to pick better.

questions: how to generate random numbers securely
subtitle: How to generate unpredictable random numbers that resist attacks by determined adversaries.

tldr.problem: Cryptographic systems depend on generating secret, unguessable random numbers, but traditional pseudo-random techniques are predictable if an adversary knows the seed or observes part of the sequence.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC explains why traditional pseudo-random generators fail, describes hardware sources of true randomness, and recommends combining multiple weak sources through strong mixing functions to achieve cryptographically strong sequences.
tldr.outcome: Systems that follow this guidance can generate truly unpredictable numbers suitable for passwords and cryptographic keys, though the RFC has been superseded by RFC 4086 which updates these recommendations.

today: RFC 1750 remains an important reference on randomness in cryptography, but has been superseded by RFC 4086 which updates the recommendations with modern cryptographic knowledge and addresses developments in random number generation techniques.

sections.title: The Randomness Problem
sections.content:
Software cryptography systems like Kerberos, PEM, and PGP provide protection against snooping and spoofing, but they depend on generating secret, unguessable (random) numbers for passwords and cryptographic keys. The security of the entire system hinges on the quality of these random quantities.

A critical requirement is that the random numbers must be resistant to attack by a resourceful and motivated adversary. Simply passing traditional statistical tests for randomness is not sufficient. An adversary with a computer and many attempts can determine secret quantities that were generated using only pseudo-random techniques seeded from limited sources like computer clocks. For example, if a 56-bit cryptographic key is generated using a pseudo-random generator seeded with only an 8-bit value, an adversary needs to search only 256 possible keys, not 2^56.

This RFC points out pitfalls in using traditional pseudo-random number generation for security and recommends techniques for producing random quantities resistant to such attacks.
sections.eli5: A computer program cannot really make truly random numbers by itself because computers are predictable. A sneaky person can guess a number if the computer picked it the normal way.

sections.title: Why Traditional Methods Fail
sections.content:
A linear congruence pseudo-random number generator uses modular arithmetic like V(n+1) = (V(n) * a + b) mod c, and similarly, linear shift register generators use XOR of bits from fixed tap positions. These methods pass traditional statistical tests and work well for simulations and games, but they completely fail for security use.

First, these sequences are fully predictable if the initial state is known. Second, depending on the form of the generator, the entire sequence may be determinable from observation of a short portion. Even revealing only one bit of the pseudo-random values allows an adversary to determine the seed from short sequences. All polynomial congruent generators have been broken by known cryptanalytic techniques.

Other weak sources include computer clocks (which provide far fewer bits of unpredictability than their specifications suggest), hardware serial numbers (which are heavily structured with limited range), and selecting from large databases (which only buys as much unpredictability as the logarithm of the number of possible starting points). The fallacy of complex manipulation is another pitfall: a very complex algorithm with a weak seed provides no real security.
sections.eli5: Computers follow rules, so anything a computer makes in a predictable way can be guessed. Even complex math does not help if the starting number is weak.

sections.title: Hardware Sources of Randomness
sections.content:
The RFC strongly recommends hardware sources of true randomness. A thermal noise or radioactive decay source combined with a fast, free-running oscillator would work directly. Any system with a spinning disk already has an adequate source of randomness due to chaotic air turbulence affecting rotational speed.

The volume of randomness required is surprisingly small. For DES (56-bit key) and highest security systems (rarely over 200 bits), only a few hundred random bits generated once a day suffice. Even if generated slowly at one bit per second, a 200-second wait is tolerable for high security applications.

Existing computer hardware can be repurposed for randomness. Sound or video input devices without sources plugged in capture thermal noise and provide reasonably high quality random bits. With compression to de-skew, one can generate huge amounts of medium-quality random data. Disk drive seek time variations include randomness that, with FFT processing, easily yields 100 bits per minute or more of excellent random data.
sections.eli5: Real random stuff from nature, like noise or how fast a disk spins, is actually random and nobody can predict it.

sections.title: Mixing Functions and De-Skewing
sections.content:
A strong mixing function combines two or more inputs and produces output where each output bit is a complex non-linear function of all input bits. On average, changing any input bit changes about half the output bits. Cryptographic functions like DES and hash functions like MD5 and SHA-1 serve as excellent mixing functions.

When hardware sources produce skewed bit streams (biased toward 0 or 1), de-skewing techniques can improve them. Simple parity (XOR of N bits) produces nearly uniform output even if individual bits are strongly biased. Von Neumann's transition mapping technique (discard 00 and 11 pairs, interpret 01 as 0 and 10 as 1) completely eliminates bias but consumes variable input bits. FFT and compression techniques can also de-skew biased streams.

The recommended non-hardware strategy is to obtain random input from a large number of uncorrelated sources and mix them with a strong mixing function. Such a function preserves randomness present in any source even if other quantities are fixed or guessable. Multiple weak sources combined with strong mixing can overcome weakness in any particular input, providing a practical approach to portable code that generates good random numbers for security.
sections.eli5: Mix together many weak random things through complicated math, and the result becomes strong and hard to predict.

sections.title: Cryptographically Strong Sequences
sections.content:
In cases where a series of random quantities must be generated, an adversary who learns some values should not be able to predict other values. The correct technique is to start with a strong random seed, take cryptographically strong steps from that seed, and not reveal the complete state of the generator in the sequence elements.

Traditional approaches hash the seed concatenated with successive integers and mask the values obtained to limit the amount of generator state available to the adversary. Alternatively, encrypt using a random key and feed some or all of the output back into the next iteration. Output feedback with shifts and masking is recommended by the US Government in connection with DES.

The Blum Blum Shub generator has the strongest public proof of strength and is based on quadratic residues. It is computationally intensive but suitable for moderately infrequent purposes like generating session keys. It allows directly calculating any value in the sequence without generating all previous values, indexed by a small number and the initial parameters.
sections.eli5: If you need many random numbers in a row, start with one good random number and do complicated math to make the next one, so knowing one does not reveal the others.

sections.title: Randomness Requirements and Standards
sections.content:
The RFC provides examples of randomness requirements for practical applications. For password generation with one try every six seconds, to have only a one-in-a-thousand chance of guessing within a year requires 29 bits of randomness. This can be achieved using US DoD recommended inputs (system clock, system ID, user ID, date and time, interrupt registers, status registers, counters, and external random input) with a DES Output Feedback Mode generator.

For very high security cryptographic keys, assuming an adversary can check 10^9 keys per second, a minimum of 51 bits is needed to ensure safety for a month. Accounting for meet-in-the-middle attacks (which can halve the exponent of work required), a doubling to 102 bits is recommended. For the highest security without special-purpose code breaking hardware, 128 bits of randomness is a good minimum for symmetric encryption keys.

The RFC also describes formal standards like the X9.17 key generation standard used by ANSI, which uses DES encryption of time values mixed with previous seed values to produce a sequence of 64-bit keys.
sections.eli5: Different jobs need different amounts of random: passwords need some, but serious codes need lots and lots.
